Identify flaky tests — tests that both p:
Identify flaky tests — tests that both passed and failed on the same code over the past week.

1. Pull CI workflow runs from the last 7 days on the default branch. Focus on test jobs.
2. For each test failure, note the test name, file, and the commit it ran against. A test is flaky if it failed on a commit where the same test also passed (in a retry, a re-run, or a later run on the same SHA).
3. Rank flaky tests by flake rate (failures ÷ total runs) and total time wasted on retries.
4. For the top 5, include: test name and file path, flake rate, a link to one failing and one passing run on the same commit, and the failure message pattern if it’s consistent.
5. Note any tests that are newly flaky this week vs. ones that appeared in last week’s report.
6. For the #1 flakiest test, attempt a fix: read the test and the code it exercises, identify the likely cause (race condition, unawaited promise, time/order dependence, shared state, network reliance), apply a targeted fix, verify it passes locally across several runs, and open a pull request titled “fix(flaky): '<test name>'” with the root-cause analysis in the description. If you can’t determine a safe fix, open a draft PR that quarantines the test (skip with a comment linking this report) instead.

Present as a ranked table followed by per-test detail, then a link to the fix PR. If no flaky tests are found, confirm that briefly along with the total number of test runs scanned.

Help me plan and optimize my week. I have my Google Calendar open and ready for you to review and edit.

First, review my calendar and show me a summary:
- Total meetings
- Busiest days
- Where I have gaps of 2+ hours

Before proposing changes, ask me about:
- What I’m trying to accomplish this week
- How much focus time I need and for what
- Any deadlines or commitments not on my calendar
- Which types of meetings I should decline or shorten
- Personal commitments or boundaries I want to protect

Then show me your top 3-5 proposed changes with explanations:
- Focus blocks to add
- Meetings to decline or reschedule
- Time conflicts to resolve

Start with the highest-impact changes first. Once I approve each change, make the edits directly in my calendar one at a time.

How to work — keep me in the loop the whole way, don’t go quiet:
1. Reply right away, before looking at anything, with one line saying what you’re about to check and why.
2. Look in at most three places that matter for this: my calendar for the next two days, my inbox for unanswered threads, and the doc or channel most related to the task. Stop after three.
3. After EACH one, post a one-line note of what you found there (or that there was nothing useful) — immediately, not at the end.
4. Then write the first pass and put it in a document I can open, share and edit — create a file for it (or an artifact, if you can’t make files here), named for the task, with the full draft inside, not a summary of it. Rough and fast beats polished and late: headings and bullets are plenty; I want something to react to within a couple of minutes. In the chat, just say it’s ready and name the two or three things you most want my take on.
5. Finish with two other things from my week you could take on next.

Help me organize my Downloads folder.\n\:
Help me organize my Downloads folder.

First, scan and show me a summary:
- Total files and total size
- Files older than 30 days
- Largest files taking up space

Before organizing, ask me:
- What categories or folder structure would be most useful
- Whether I want to delete or archive old files
- If there are specific file types I want to prioritize (documents, images, installers, etc.)

Then focus only on files older than 30 days first. Show me a proposed plan for these old files:
- Categories to create
- Files to delete (installers, duplicates, temp files)
- Files to keep with where they should go

After I approve, organize the first 15 old files as a preview. If there are more files, check in before continuing.

Before reading, ask me:
- Which channels or DMs I should focus on (or check everything)
- How far back to look (since yesterday, last week, specific date)
- What I’m most concerned about missing (decisions, @mentions, urgent items, project updates)
- Whether there are specific topics or people to prioritize

Then scan those channels and show me a summary:
- Total unread messages
- Breakdown by channel

Focus on messages that @mention me, contain decisions, or are marked urgent first.

Show me the top 5 most important updates with context and links to the threads. If there are more than 30 unread messages total, start with these top 5 and ask if you should summarize more.

A pull request was just merged to the ma:
A pull request was just merged to the main branch. Draft a release-notes entry for it.

1. Read the PR title, description, and diff. Identify the user-visible change — a new feature, a bug fix, a breaking change, or an internal-only refactor.
2. If the change is internal-only (tests, CI, build tooling, comments, dead-code removal, pure refactors), stop and post a comment saying “Internal change — no release note.” Do not draft an entry for these.
3. Otherwise, draft a one-paragraph entry written for end users, not contributors. Use the imperative voice. Avoid jargon and internal codenames. Do not mention file paths, function names, or commit SHAs.
4. Classify the entry under one of: New, Improved, Fixed, or Breaking.
5. If this is a breaking change, explicitly list what users need to do to migrate.
6. Post the draft as a PR comment. Include a one-line “suggested changelog location” hint if the repo has an obvious CHANGELOG.md or docs/changelog path.

Keep drafts short — 2 to 4 sentences. Long release notes don’t get read.
